entry: Large cat (*Panthera leo*) of the genus *Panthera*, now native only to [[Sub-Saharan Africa|sub-Saharan Africa]] and [[India]]. Adult males are larger than females and have a prominent mane extending from the head to the shoulders and chest. Lions are a social species, forming groups called prides of related females, their cubs and one or a few unrelated adult males. The lion is an [[Apex predator|apex]] and keystone predator, preying mostly on medium-sized and large [[Ungulate|hoofed mammals]] in [[Grassland|grasslands]], savannas and shrublands. During the [[Neolithic]] period it ranged across Africa and [[Eurasia]], from southeastern Europe to India. Populations in African countries declined by about 43% since the early 1990s, and the species has been listed as Vulnerable on the Red List of the International Union for Conservation of Nature since 1996. Habitat loss and conflict with humans are the main concerns. Lions have long been depicted as symbols of power and royalty.

Argentine footballer and forward for Inter Miami in [[Major League Soccer]]. Messi played for [[FC Barcelona|Barcelona]] from 2004 to 2021, becoming the club's all-time top scorer and winning 10 [[La Liga]] titles and four [[UEFA Champions League]] trophies. He then won two Ligue 1 titles with Paris Saint-Germain and joined Inter Miami in 2023, leading it to its first MLS Cup in 2025 and winning the league MVP award in 2024 and 2025. He is the most decorated player in professional football history, with 47 team trophies across more than 1,200 career appearances, With the [[Argentina national football team|Argentina national team]], he is the all-time leading goalscorer (126) and most-capped player (208). He won the gold medal at the 2008 Summer Olympics and led the team to victory at the 2021 [[Copa América]], the 2022 FIFA World Cup and the 2024 Copa América. He retired from international football again in October 2026.

American singer, songwriter and record producer. Richie rose to fame as co-lead singer and songwriter of the [[Motown]] group the Commodores before launching a solo career in 1982. His album *Can't Slow Down* (1983) reached number one on the U.S. Billboard 200 and sold over 20 million copies. He co-wrote the charity single "[[We Are the World]]" (1985) with [[Michael Jackson]], which sold over 20 million copies and won a [[Grammy Awards|Grammy]] for Song of the Year. He has sold over 90 million records and has been a judge on [[American Idol]] since 2018.

Genus (*Pterois*) of venomous marine fish native to Indo-Pacific [[Coral reef|coral reefs]]. Lionfish have conspicuous red or black bands and dorsal fins tipped with venomous spines, which are their main defense against predators. Five species are recognized, and *Pterois radiata*, *P. volitans* and *P. miles* are the most studied; several are popular aquarium fish. *P. volitans* and *P. miles* are [[Invasive species|invasive]] in the western Atlantic, the [[Caribbean Sea|Caribbean]] and the [[Mediterranean Sea]]. Females can lay about 2 million eggs per year. Lionfish prey mostly on small fish, invertebrates and mollusks.

Flat-panel display that uses the light-modulating properties of liquid crystals combined with [[Polarizer|polarizers]]. Liquid crystals do not emit light, so a liquid-crystal display (LCD) relies on a backlight or reflector to produce images in color or monochrome. Arbitrary images are formed from a matrix of small [[Pixel|pixels]], while simpler devices such as digital clocks show preset digits or words. LCDs appear in [[Computer monitor|computer monitors]], televisions, instrument panels, aircraft cockpit displays and signage, as well as in [[Calculator|calculators]], [[Watch|watches]] and [[Smartphone|smartphones]]. They replaced bulky cathode-ray tube displays in nearly all applications from the late 2000s to the early 2010s. LCDs are not subject to screen burn-in, but they are susceptible to image persistence.

Nitrogen in liquid form, with a [[Boiling point|boiling point]] of about −196 °C (77 K). It is produced industrially by [[Distillation|fractional distillation]] of liquid air. The colorless liquid has a [[Viscosity|viscosity]] about half that of [[Acetone]], and it is widely used as a coolant. It boils immediately on contact with warmer objects, enveloping them in insulating gas bubbles. Its low boiling point results from weak intermolecular attraction. Applications include cryotherapy to remove [[Wart|warts]] and other skin lesions, cryopreservation of blood and [[Sperm|sperm]] and egg cells, and the freezing of food. Because it rapidly freezes living tissue, it must be stored in vacuum flasks.

Alcoholic drink produced by [[Distillation|distilling]] fermented grains, fruits, vegetables or sugar. The word usually refers to distilled spirits, which contain much more alcohol than [[Beer]] and wine; those typically reach at most about 15% alcohol by volume. Liquor without added sugar is called a spirit and is usually 35–40% alcohol by volume, while sweetened, flavored versions are liqueurs. Many liquors are aged in barrels, as [[Brandy]], tequila and whiskey are, and others, such as absinthe, are infused with flavorings. Liquor is often drunk neat, in servings of about 50 milliliters, or mixed into [[Cocktail|cocktails]]. Rapid consumption of large amounts can cause alcohol poisoning, and all alcohol is classed as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer.

Sweet, aromatic flavoring extracted from the root of *Glycyrrhiza glabra*, a [[Fabaceae|bean family]] plant. The herbaceous perennial is native to [[West Asia]], tropical Asia, North Africa and southern Europe. Its root contains glycyrrhizin, which has 30–50 times the sweetness of sugar. Licorice is used as a flavoring in confectionery, [[Tobacco|tobacco]], beverages and pharmaceuticals, and is marketed as a [[Dietary supplement|dietary supplement]]. Extracts have been used in [[Traditional medicine|traditional medicine]]. Excessive consumption of more than 2 mg/kg [0.91 mg/lb] per day of pure glycyrrhizinic acid can lead to [[Hypertension|hypertension]], low blood potassium and muscle weakness, and licorice root extract should be avoided during pregnancy.

American actress, writer and producer. Kudrow is best known for playing Phoebe Buffay in the [[NBC]] sitcom *Friends* (1994–2004). She began in improv comedy with The Groundlings in Los Angeles and played Ursula Buffay in *Mad About You*. She starred as Valerie Cherish in the [[HBO]] mockumentary *The Comeback* (2005–2026). Her films include *Romy and Michele's High School Reunion* (1997) and *The Opposite of Sex* (1998). Her accolades include a Primetime Emmy Award and two Actor Awards.

Taiwanese and American business executive, computer scientist and electrical engineer. Su has been president and chief executive officer of [[AMD]] since 2014. Born in Taiwan, she immigrated to the United States as a young child and earned three degrees from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. She then held engineering and management posts at Texas Instruments, [[IBM]] and Freescale Semiconductor. At IBM she helped develop silicon-on-insulator manufacturing technologies. During her tenure at AMD, the company's market capitalization grew from roughly $3 billion to more than $1 trillion. She was the first woman named [[Time (magazine)|Time]] CEO of the Year, in 2014, and was named again in 2024.

Capital and most populous city of [[Portugal]] (pop., 2025: 658,236). Lisbon lies on the northern shore of the River Tagus and is the second-oldest European capital, after [[Athens]]. Founded by the Phoenicians, it was made a municipium by [[Julius Caesar]], was ruled by the [[Visigoths]], and was captured by the [[Moors]] in the 8th century. Afonso Henriques conquered it in 1147, and in 1255 it replaced Coimbra as Portugal's capital. The city hosts the government, the Assembly of the Republic, the Supreme Court of Justice and the residence of the head of state. Its metropolitan area has 3,353,000 people, the third largest in the [[Iberian Peninsula]] after Madrid and Barcelona.

Austrian and Swedish nuclear physicist. Meitner earned a doctorate in physics from the [[University of Vienna]] in 1906, becoming the second woman to do so there. She lost her positions in Berlin in 1935 under the anti-Jewish Nuremberg Laws of [[Nazi Germany]] and fled to the Netherlands in 1938. In late December 1938 she worked with her nephew Otto Robert Frisch to interpret experiments by [[Otto Hahn]] and Fritz Strassmann showing that neutron bombardment of [[Uranium]] produced barium. They named the process fission in 1939. Hahn received the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery, and Meitner did not share it. She had been nominated 19 times for the chemistry prize (1924–1948) and 30 times for physics (1937–1967). Several scientists and journalists have called her exclusion "unjust". Element 109, meitnerium, was named for her in 1997.

Family of programming languages distinguished by a fully parenthesized prefix notation. Originally specified in the late 1950s, Lisp is the second-oldest high-level programming language still in common use, after [[Fortran]]. John McCarthy began developing it in 1958 at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. Lisp programs can manipulate source code as data, which enables macros. It pioneered tree data structures, automatic storage management, dynamic typing and [[Recursion|recursion]], and it became a favored language for [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] research. The best-known general-purpose dialects are Common Lisp, Scheme, Racket and Clojure.

headword: List of unsolved problems in physics
sort_key: list of unsolved problems in physics
entry: Overview of major open questions in physics.Open questions beyond the [[Standard Model]] include the strong CP problem, the absolute mass of neutrinos, matter–antimatter asymmetry, and the nature of [[Dark matter]] and [[Dark energy]]. The Standard Model is also inconsistent with [[General relativity]], and the two theories break down under extreme conditions, such as at the [[Big Bang]] and at the centers of [[Black hole|black holes]]. In 1900, [[Lord Kelvin]] identified two "clouds" over physics; both were resolved within a decade by special relativity and quantum mechanics. The Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the [[Millennium Prize Problems]], remains unsolved.

Study, evaluation and interpretation of [[Literature|literature]]. It is often closely tied to literary theory, the philosophical analysis of literature's goals and methods, although critics are not always theorists. Critics publish essays and books, teach in academic departments, or write reviews for periodicals such as *The New York Review of Books* and *The New Yorker*. Literary criticism is thought to have existed as far back as the [[Classical antiquity|classical period]]. In the 4th century BC, [[Aristotle]] wrote the *Poetics*, which developed the concepts of mimesis and catharsis. Aristotle's work was the most important influence on literary criticism until the late eighteenth century. In 1498, Giorgio Valla published a Latin translation of the *Poetics*, marking the birth of Renaissance criticism.

Chemical element with symbol Li and atomic number 3, a soft, silvery-white [[Alkali metal|alkali metal]]. It is the least dense metal and solid element under standard conditions and is highly reactive, so it is stored in inert liquids such as purified [[Kerosene|kerosene]] or mineral oil. Lithium occurs mainly in pegmatitic minerals and in brines. Its name derives from the Ancient Greek word for stone. In 1932 the transmutation of lithium atoms to [[Helium]] was the first fully human-made nuclear reaction, and lithium deuteride serves as a fusion fuel in thermonuclear weapons. Batteries consume more than three-quarters of lithium production. Lithium-based drugs are used as a mood stabilizer and antidepressant in treating [[Bipolar disorder|bipolar disorder]].

Rechargeable battery that stores energy through the reversible intercalation of [[Lithium|lithium]] ions into solids. It has higher energy density and longer cycle life than other rechargeable types. Commercialized by a [[Sony]] and Asahi Kasei team in 1991, it powers portable electronics, laptops, phones and electric cars, and is used for grid-scale storage. In three decades its volumetric energy density increased threefold while its cost dropped tenfold. John Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino received the 2019 [[Nobel Prize]] in Chemistry for its development. Its flammable electrolyte poses fire risks, and solid-state designs are in development.

Rigid outermost rocky shell of a [[Terrestrial planet|terrestrial planet]] or [[Natural satellite|natural satellite]]. On Earth it consists of the crust and the lithospheric mantle, the uppermost part of the mantle, which behaves elastically over time scales of up to thousands of years or more. It lies above the weaker, hotter asthenosphere, and their boundary is set by the temperature at which [[Olivine|olivine]] becomes ductile, about 1,000 °C (1,830 °F). Earth's lithosphere is divided into [[Plate tectonics|tectonic plates]]. The term was introduced by the American geologist Joseph Barrell. Oceanic lithosphere thickens as it ages and moves away from [[Mid-ocean ridge|mid-ocean ridges]], and the oldest is typically about 140 kilometers thick.

Country on the eastern shore of the [[Baltic Sea]] in northern Europe. Its capital and largest city is [[Vilnius]], and it covers 65,300 sq km. Mindaugas united Lithuanian lands and formed the Kingdom of Lithuania on 6 July 1253. By the 14th century the [[Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] was the largest country in Europe. In 1569 it united with Poland as the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, which lasted more than two centuries until neighboring countries dismantled it between 1772 and 1795. Lithuania declared independence in 1918. It was occupied by the [[Soviet Union]] and then [[Nazi Germany]] in [[World War II]], and was reoccupied by the Soviets in 1944. On 11 March 1990 it became the first Soviet republic to proclaim the restoration of its independence. Lithuania is a high-income economy and a member of the [[European Union]] and [[NATO]].

Metric unit of volume equal to one cubic decimeter, or 1,000 cubic centimeters. The liter is not an [[International System of Units|SI]] unit, which uses the cubic meter; one liter equals 0.001 cubic meter. The spelling "litre" is used by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures and most English-speaking countries, while "liter" predominates in American English. From 1901 to 1964 the liter was defined as the volume of one kilogram of pure [[Water|water]] at maximum density (+3.98 °C). Water still has a mass of almost exactly one [[Kilogram|kilogram]] per liter, because the kilogram was defined in 1795 as the mass of one cubic decimeter of water at 0 °C. Liters are most commonly used for fluids and other items measured by container capacity.

Series of American children's novels by [[Laura Ingalls Wilder]], and its media franchise. The books draw on Wilder's childhood in the Midwest between 1872 and 1894. The first, *Little House in the Big Woods*, appeared in 1932 from Harper & Brothers. Eight novels were completed in Wilder's lifetime, and the third is also titled *Little House on the Prairie*. A ninth draft was published posthumously in 1971, and the diary *On the Way Home* (1962) covers the years after 1894. The books have sold around 60 million copies. The American television series *Little House on the Prairie* ran from 1974 to 1983.

Period of regional cooling, most pronounced in the North Atlantic region, conventionally dated from the 16th to the 19th centuries. It was not a true ice age of global extent, and the term was introduced by François E. Matthes in 1939. Some experts prefer a span from about 1300 to about 1850. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's Third Assessment Report described the Northern Hemisphere as modestly cooled, by less than 1°C relative to late twentieth-century levels. Proposed causes include lows in solar radiation, heightened volcanic activity, changes in ocean circulation, variations in Earth's orbit and axial tilt, and population declines from events such as the [[Black Death]]. In the 13th century, pack ice advanced southward in the North Atlantic, as did glaciers in [[Greenland]].

European fairy tale about a young girl and a Big Bad Wolf. Its origins lie in several folk tales from before the 17th century. It was first recorded in literary form in French by [[Charles Perrault]], whose version ends with the wolf eating the girl. Later versions, including those of the [[Brothers Grimm]], add a woodcutter or hunter who rescues the girl and her grandmother. In the Grimms' version, the wolf tries to drink from a well, falls in because of the stones in its stomach, and drowns. The tale is number 333 in the Aarne–Thompson classification of folktales.

American singer, pianist and songwriter, called the "Architect of Rock and Roll." Born Richard Wayne Penniman in Macon, Georgia, he was an influential figure in popular music for seven decades. His frenetic piano playing, pounding backbeat and raspy vocals in the mid-1950s laid the foundation for [[Rock and roll|rock and roll]]. "Tutti Frutti" (1955) crossed over to the pop charts, and "Long Tall Sally" (1956) reached number one on the Billboard Rhythm and Blues chart. He influenced [[Rhythm and blues|rhythm and blues]], soul and funk. After a five-year period in which he abandoned rock and roll for born-again Christianity, he returned in 1962 to tour Europe, where [[The Beatles|the Beatles]] opened for him on some dates. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1986 as one of its first inductees.

Capital and most populous city of the U.S. state of [[Arkansas]] (pop., 2020: 202,591) and county seat of Pulaski County. The city lies on the south bank of the Arkansas River. It was founded in 1821 as the capital of the Arkansas Territory and is named for a rock formation on the river that the French explorer Jean-Baptiste Bénard de la Harpe named in 1722. The 1957 desegregation of Little Rock Central High School was a key event in the [[Civil rights movement|Civil Rights movement]]. The metropolitan area has an estimated 770,000 residents. Dillard's and Windstream Holdings are headquartered in the city.
